turns.content: My closest friend from college called last night. His father needs a procedure — real thing, I've known uncle for years — and he asked me for eighty thousand, "just for two months." Here's the thing I didn't say: in 2019 I gave him fifty thousand. Neither of us has mentioned it since. Not once, not him, not me.

Oh, wow. That is an incredibly heavy position to be put in, and my heart goes out to you. It’s not just about the money; it’s about the silence that’s been sitting between you for years.

The fact that you didn’t mention the 2019 loan back then—and he hasn’t either—creates a really complicated dynamic. It sounds like there’s a pattern of avoiding the "real talk" in your friendship, and that silence has now become a wall.

If I were in your shoes, I’d be feeling a mix of genuine worry for his father and a lot of frustration about being put in this spot again.

Are you leaning toward saying no? Because if you are, you’re well within your rights to do so. That previous debt is a massive elephant in the room that he is choosing to ignore, and you aren't a bank.

If you *do* decide to talk to him, do you think you’re ready to finally break that silence about the 2019 money? It feels like you can’t address this new request without addressing the old one. How are you feeling about the idea of actually bringing it up with him?

Meanwhile I'm eleven months into saving for a flat down payment. And my wife doesn't know about the 2019 money — it was before the wedding and it just... never came up, and now it's a thing I've apparently decided not to tell her, which I hate. If I move eighty thousand she will definitely notice.

That adds a whole new layer of pressure. It’s not just about the money anymore; it’s about your future, your marriage, and the secrets that are starting to pile up.

Honestly? The fact that your wife would definitely notice an 80k transfer is a huge flashing light. It’s not just a "financial decision" at that point; it’s a decision that impacts your life together. If you were to give him that money, you’d be keeping a secret from her that you already feel guilty about, and you’d be actively setting back the goal you two are working toward.

It sounds like you’re carrying the weight of his problem, the weight of the past debt, *and* the weight of this secret, all on your own. That is a massive burden for one person to hold.

When you say you "hate" that you never told her, does that feel like a nudge to finally be honest? Maybe not necessarily about the 2019 money right this second, but about the situation *now*?

If you were to tell your wife, "Hey, my friend is in a tough spot and asked for a loan, and I'm really struggling with how to handle it," would that feel like a relief? It might be the only way to get some clarity. It’s hard to carry a secret that big in a marriage—it creates distance, even if you don't mean for it to.

How do you think she would react if you brought the request to her, rather than trying to handle it in the shadows?

I was thinking I'll tell him my money is parked in FDs and mutual funds, all locked in, nothing liquid. It's a small lie and it saves the friendship — he keeps his respect, I keep my savings, nobody has to say the real sentence. Is that wrong? It feels smart and it also feels a bit sick.

It makes sense why you’d feel that way. It *is* a smart short-term fix—it’s a "clean" exit that avoids the messiness of bringing up 2019 or having to say "no" directly. It protects his pride and avoids the awkwardness.

But the reason it feels "sick" is that it doesn’t actually solve the problem; it just masks it.

By using the "my money is locked away" excuse, you’re choosing to stay in a dynamic where you are the silent enabler and he is the person who gets to ignore his own history. You’re essentially agreeing to keep the relationship shallow to keep it "easy."

Here is the thing to consider: if you tell this lie, you are cementing the dynamic where you can’t be honest with him. You’re effectively saying, "I value the *appearance* of our friendship more than I value *truth* in our friendship."

Is it "wrong"? Not in the sense that you’re a bad person for wanting to avoid an agonizing conflict. We all protect ourselves. But ask yourself: **If you lie to him now, will you ever be able to trust him again?** Every time you see him, you’ll know that you had to trick him to get him to respect your boundaries. That doesn't really feel like a friendship—it feels like a negotiation.

Also, consider the risk: What if he says, "Oh, I understand, maybe you could help me figure out how to liquidate one, or maybe you could ask your wife?" Suddenly, your "small lie" could snowball into a much bigger, more complicated one.

If you aren't ready to have the "Real Talk" about 2019, maybe there’s a middle ground? You could say something like, "I'm so sorry about your dad, but I’ve committed all my available savings toward our flat down payment. I really can't touch that money right now."

That’s the truth. It doesn't require lying about FDs, it doesn't require bringing up the 2019 debt, and it sets a firm boundary. It’s honest, it’s adult, and it doesn't force you to play games. How does that feel compared to the "locked in" lie?

The part that actually keeps me up: someday he'll be standing in my flat at the housewarming, hugging me, and some part of me will still be doing 2019's math. I don't want to become that person — the friend with a ledger in his chest. But I also can't keep being the guy whose money is everyone's buffer.
That image of "a ledger in your chest" is haunting, and it’s the most honest thing you’ve said yet. It really cuts to the core of why this is eating you alive.
